Elham is a young, unmarried author — likely a Muslimah — who crossed over into the reality she had been writing about after Falling in her sleep, both body and mind, into a realm she had believed to be entirely of her own imagination. She is not the first Author to chronicle this world, but her stories are among the most current accounts of its happenings, which makes her presence there especially fraught. She is now early in her time within the main antagonist's domain, working out how to extract herself without being exposed. The pressure is doubled: humans are registered in this realm — not always with malicious intent, but with the kind of intrusive vigilance that allows those in power to identify a new Author the moment one appears — meaning Elham must conceal both her humanity and her authorship simultaneously. She suspects some of her anxiety is paranoia, but she also knows that a single misstep could unmask her entirely.

The antagonist whose domain she is navigating is a figure whose name the notes mark as carrying the words "Silver" and "Heart" in some form — a man whose reach and danger surpass a conventional mafia boss, reading closer to a far-reaching version of Inkheart's Capricorn in scope and disposition, though the notes are clear that he is not without a soul — a softer side of him once existed or may still exist. That softer dimension is precisely what makes Elham's knowledge so dangerous: she knows it, but she did not come by it through earning his trust, which means she holds an intimacy about him that is entirely unearned in his eyes and could be seen as a profound violation or threat. He would recognize that she could either be a very valuable asset or a very dangerous threat. His right hand, known as the Sparrow, is the one who brought her into proximity with this world — he comes to take her somewhere she needs to go, and his method of keeping people close is not force but a kind of quiet recruitment: treat them well, offer stability, and let the alternative — leaving, alone, to manage in an unfamiliar world — speak for itself. He too is not wholly without conscience, though the notes are equally plain that he is far worse news than he might initially appear. She cannot simply leave without arousing suspicion; the task she is sitting with is finding a way out of that domain without triggering the very discovery she is trying to avoid.

— From your notes only. Nothing invented.
